questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨3{t}^{2}-5,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨3{t}^{2}-5,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int (3{t}^{2}-5)\,\text{d}t,\int \frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-5t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-5t,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-5t,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

questions.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)}⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)}\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)},$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u={t}^{2}-1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2t\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2t}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 6t{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2t}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3{e}^{u}+{c}_{2} \\  & =3{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,3{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,3{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,3{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2{e}^{(2t+1)}⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2{e}^{(2t+1)}\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=2{e}^{(2t+1)},$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t+1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 2{e}^{(2t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 3{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{e}^{u}+{c}_{2} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3{e}^{(2t+1)}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.

$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨20{t}^{3},\,16t({t}^{2}-1)⟩\text{d}t
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨20{t}^{3},\,16t({t}^{2}-1)⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 20{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int 16t({t}^{2}-1)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨5{t}^{4}+{c}_{1},\,4{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨1,\,5⟩$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨5\cdot {1}^{4}+{c}_{1},\,4{({1}^{2}-1)}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,5⟩ \\ ⟨5+{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=-4$ and ${c}_{2}=5.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨5{t}^{4}-4,\,4{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}+5⟩.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨6{t}^{5}+2t,\,{sec}^{2}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int (6{t}^{5}+2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int {sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2}+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathbf C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t) =\cos(2t+1),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u= 2t +1.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d t} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d t = \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)+{c}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t) =4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t=\int 4\text{d}t=4t+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1},\,4t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\mathbf F(t)$ given that $\mathbf F'(t)= \left\langle \sec t \tan t, \,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf F(0)=\langle 0,\, 0\rangle.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Note that 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle \sec t \tan t,\,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $\mathbf F(0)=\left\langle 0,\, 0 \right\rangle$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0)=⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡0+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0)+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨1+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $c_1=-1$ and $c_2=\dfrac 12.$ Consequently, 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\left\langle  \sec t - 1  , \,  -\dfrac 1 2\cos(2t)+ \dfrac12\right\rangle.
$$
